pos: n. pl. (a Canaanite people of the hill country — in Scripture the standing name for the whole population God dispossessed, and the standing measure of a nation's ripening guilt)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Emori, from a root meaning to say or to be prominent; the Akkadian Amurru named both a people and the westward direction, so the name carries the sense of the highlanders of the west.
biblical_def: The Amorites were one of the seven nations of Canaan, settled chiefly in the hill country on both sides of Jordan, and their name is used so broadly that it often stands for the whole Canaanite population together. Two texts make them theologically decisive. The first is Gen 15:16, where the LORD tells Abraham that his seed must wait four generations “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full” — a sentence that settles once for all how the conquest is to be read. Israel does not take Canaan because Israel is worthier; Israel takes Canaan as the LORD's instrument of judgment upon a guilt that has been accumulating, patiently borne, and finally measured to the brim. The second is Amo 2:9, where the LORD recalls destroying the Amorite “whose height was like the height of the cedars” — the giant-stature memory that made the ten spies faint. Their gods are the alternative Joshua sets before the tribes at Shechem: serve the LORD, or serve “the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell” (Jos 24:15). Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, the two Amorite kings east of Jordan, become Israel's standing psalmody of victory (Psa 135:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no separate article for the Amorites; the 1828 dictionary treats Canaanite peoples under the general head of the nations of Canaan, and the biblical usage governs.
webster_full: AMORITE, n. One of a people descended from Emor or Amor, the fourth son of Canaan; a Canaanitish nation inhabiting the mountain country.
The name is used in Scripture both of a particular tribe and, by synecdoche, of the Canaanite nations generally.
In Gen. xv. 16 the iniquity of the Amorites is set as the measure of the time appointed for Israel's return.
Their two kings east of Jordan, Sihon and Og, were subdued by Moses before the passage of the river.
Their remnant was reduced to bond-service under Solomon.
scriptures: But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.
Amo 2:9
Yet destroyed I the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars, and he was strong as the oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
But thou shalt utterly destroy them; namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee:
corruption_summary: The conquest is read as ethnic cleansing by a tribal deity, which requires ignoring the one verse that explains it — the four-generation delay for a guilt not yet full.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection to the conquest treats Canaan as innocent land seized by an invading people, and it can only be maintained by leaving Gen 15:16 out of the account. Scripture states the ground plainly: the dispossession is judicial, it waits four generations for the guilt to ripen, and the same law that expelled the Amorite is expressly threatened against Israel if Israel does the same things — “that the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you” (Lev 18:28). A judgment that falls impartially on the covenant nation is not tribalism. Deu 9:5 forecloses the other reading: Israel enters “not for thy righteousness” but for the wickedness of those nations and for the oath sworn to the fathers.

There is a second and gentler corruption, common in preaching: turning the Amorites into a symbol of personal besetting sins and losing the history altogether. The allegory is not wrong, but it is parasitic on the fact. If the Amorites were never a real people whose real guilt was really measured, then the patience of God recorded in Gen 15:16 is a fiction, and so is the warning that patience has an end. Recover the fact first, and the application follows: God bears long with nations, keeps the account exactly, and closes it at the hour He appointed.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Emori (H567), Amorite, from 'amar (H559), to say or speak, or from a cognate sense of height and prominence; Akkadian Amurru, the west.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Emori (H567) — Amorite; the gentilic of Emor, fourth son of Canaan (Gen 10:16).
Hebrew 'amar (H559) — to say; the likeliest root, though the sense of prominence or height suits Amo 2:9 and the giant tradition.
Hebrew 'awon (H5771) — iniquity; the word measured in Gen 15:16, guilt reckoned as a quantity that fills.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to dispossess, to take as an inheritance; the verb of the conquest, judicial and covenantal at once.
Hebrew Sichon (H5511) — Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon whose defeat became a refrain of praise (Psa 136:19).
usage: “The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full” — the clock by which the exodus was timed.
“The gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell” — Joshua's alternative at Shechem.
“Whose height was like the height of the cedars” — the giants the LORD felled.

pos: n. pl. (the children of Heth — a great northern power in the land, and the people from whom Abraham bought a grave and David stole a wife)
etymology: From Hebrew Chitti, the gentilic of Cheth (Heth), second son of Canaan (Gen 10:15). The same people appear in cuneiform as Hatti, an empire centred in Asia Minor whose southern reach touched Canaan.
biblical_def: The Hittites stand in every list of the nations of Canaan, and Jos 1:4 measures the promised territory as “all the land of the Hittites” — a phrase that tells how large their name loomed. Scripture meets them at two unforgettable points. The first is a funeral: Abraham, a stranger and sojourner with no ground of his own, comes to the children of Heth at the gate of Hebron and buys the cave of Machpelah for a burying place, paying four hundred shekels in the hearing of the city rather than accept it as a gift (Gen 23:10ff). It is the patriarch's only freehold in the land of promise, and it is a grave — faith holding a title deed to a resurrection it will not live to see. The second is an adultery: “Uriah the Hittite” (2Sa 11:3), the foreigner whose loyalty to the ark and to his fellow soldiers shames the king of Israel, and whose murder is the blackest page in David's life. Between these two the Hittites are named as one of the seven nations to be driven out (Deu 20:17), and yet they furnish both the seller of a saint's grave and one of David's mighty men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats the Hittites under the Canaanite nations, deriving the name from Heth, the son of Canaan, and noting their settlement about Hebron and northward.
webster_full: HITTITE, n. A descendant of Heth, the second son of Canaan; one of the seven nations of the land of Canaan.
The children of Heth dwelt about Hebron, where Abraham purchased of them the field and cave of Machpelah.
The name is also used of a northern power whose land bounded the promise on the north (Josh. i. 4).
Esau took wives of the daughters of Heth, to the grief of Isaac and Rebekah.
Uriah, one of David's worthies, was a Hittite.
scriptures: Jos 1:4
From the wilderness and this Lebanon even unto the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, and unto the great sea toward the going down of the sun, shall be your coast.
And Ephron dwelt among the children of Heth: and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the audience of the children of Heth, even of all that went in at the gate of his city, saying,
And David sent and enquired after the woman. And one said, Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?
Exo 3:8

And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey; unto the place of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
corruption_summary: For a century the Hittites were cited as proof that the Bible invented nations; the spade answered, and the lesson — absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — is still resisted.
corruption_paragraphs: Before the excavations at Boghazkoy the Hittites were a standing exhibit in the case against Scripture's historical reliability: no such empire was known outside the Bible, therefore the Bible had manufactured them. Then the archives came out of the ground, and an empire appeared that had treated with Egypt as an equal. The right conclusion was not that archaeology validates Scripture — Scripture is not on probation before the spade, and its authority rests on the God who spoke it — but that silence proves nothing, and that the confident negative verdicts of one generation are routinely buried by the next. The pattern has repeated with Belshazzar, with the house of David inscription, with Pontius Pilate's stone.

The living temptation the Hittites expose is different: Esau “took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite” (Gen 26:34), and they “were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.” Marriage across the covenant line is the way the nations that could not conquer Israel entered Israel anyway. The New Testament keeps the principle without the ethnicity — “only in the Lord” (1Co 7:39), “be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14). What Canaan could not take by the sword it took by the wedding.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chitti (H2850), Hittite, from Cheth (H2845), Heth; cognate with Akkadian and Egyptian Hatti.
roots_lines: Hebrew Cheth (H2845) — Heth, second son of Canaan, ancestor of the people (Gen 10:15).
Hebrew Chitti (H2850) — Hittite; used both of the Hebron clan and of the northern power.
Hebrew bene-Cheth — “children of Heth”, the phrase of Gen 23, a lawful assembly at the city gate.
Hebrew 'achuzzath-qeber (H272 + H6913) — a possession of a buryingplace; Abraham's single holding in Canaan.
Hebrew ger we-toshab (H1616 + H8453) — “a stranger and a sojourner”, Abraham's self-description before them (Gen 23:4).
usage: “All the land of the Hittites” — the northern measure of the promise.
“Uriah the Hittite” — the foreigner whose integrity indicted a king.
“The children of Heth” — the assembly at the gate that sold Abraham a grave.

pos: n. pl. (a people of Canaan, named in every conquest list and in no genealogy — the villagers of the open country)
etymology: From Hebrew Perizzi, probably from perazi, dwelling in unwalled villages, from paraz, to separate or to be open. Unlike the Hittites and Amorites they are not traced to a son of Canaan in Gen 10, which fits a name that describes a manner of dwelling rather than a lineage.
biblical_def: The Perizzites are the quiet name in the lists. They appear in every roll of the nations Israel was to dispossess (Deu 20:17; Jos 3:10; Neh 9:8), yet they are absent from the table of nations in Gen 10, and Scripture gives them no king, no capital, and no single battle of their own. What it gives them is a location: they are the people of the open country, the unwalled villages scattered between the fortified towns, and their standing phrase pairs them with the Canaanites — “the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land” (Gen 13:7). That verse is the setting of Abram's quarrel with Lot; the presence of watching pagans is precisely why the strife between brethren was intolerable. Jacob names them again when Simeon and Levi have made the family a stench “among the Canaanites and the Perizzites” (Gen 34:30). Judah defeats them at Bezek (Jdg 1:4), and centuries later Ezra finds the returned exiles married into them still (Ezr 9:1). They are the people who never went away — not conquered by a decisive stroke, simply absorbed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) lists the Perizzites among the Canaanitish nations, noting the derivation from a word signifying villagers or dwellers in the open country.
webster_full: PERIZZITE, n. One of a Canaanitish people dwelling in the land promised to Abraham.
The name is thought to signify a villager, or one dwelling in an unwalled town, from a root denoting openness.
They are not reckoned among the sons of Canaan in the tenth of Genesis, yet are named in every enumeration of the nations to be driven out.
They dwelt intermixed with the Canaanites, chiefly in the wooded hill country.
Their remnant remained in the land to the days of Ezra, and Israel had married among them.
scriptures: Gen 13:7
And there was a strife between the herdmen of Abram's cattle and the herdmen of Lot's cattle: and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.

And Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, Ye have troubled me to make me to stink among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites: and I being few in number, they shall gather themselves together against me, and slay me; and I shall be destroyed, I and my house.
Jdg 1:4
And Judah went up; and the LORD delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand: and they slew of them in Bezek ten thousand men.
Ezr 9:1

Now when these things were done, the princes came to me, saying, The people of Israel, and the priests, and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the people of the lands, doing according to their abominations, even of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites.
corruption_summary: An enemy with no fortress and no king is the one Israel never finished driving out; the sins that ruin a soul are likewise the diffuse ones that never present a wall to storm.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the Perizzites illustrate by being unremarkable. Israel could muster for Jericho because Jericho had walls; the villagers of the open country offered nothing to besiege, and so Israel simply settled down beside them, and by Ezra's day the covenant people were marrying them. Scripture's hardest commands are seldom about the visible fortress. “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” (Col 3:5) names things with no walls: covetousness, inordinate affection, the small permanent neighbours of the soul.

Gen 13:7 supplies the second lesson, and it is a sharp one for the church. The reason Abram would not tolerate strife with Lot is stated in the same breath as the strife: “and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.” The world was watching. Paul reasons identically about brethren going to law before unbelievers — “there is utterly a fault among you” (1Co 6:7). Quarrelling saints do their damage chiefly in front of the Perizzites.
roots_summary: Hebrew Perizzi (H6522), Perizzite, from perazi (H6521), a villager, and perazah (H6519), an unwalled town, from paraz, to separate or spread out.
roots_lines: Hebrew Perizzi (H6522) — Perizzite; the gentilic used in all seven-nation lists.
Hebrew perazi (H6521) — a rustic, one who dwells in the open country without walls.
Hebrew perazah (H6519) — an unwalled village; used of Jerusalem restored, “inhabited as towns without walls” (Zec 2:4).
Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to dwell, to sit down; the verb of Gen 13:7, quiet permanent settlement.
Hebrew badal (H914) — to separate; the word Ezra uses of what Israel failed to do (Ezr 9:1).
usage: “The Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land” — the watching world behind a family quarrel.
“Among the Canaanites and the Perizzites” — Jacob counting the cost of his sons' revenge.
“Have not separated themselves” — Ezra's verdict a thousand years later.

pos: n. pl. (a Canaanite people descended from Canaan — the nation of Shechem's outrage, and the only nation that made peace with Israel)
etymology: From Hebrew Chiwwi, the gentilic of a name possibly connected with chawwah, a tent-village or encampment; if so the Hivites, like the Perizzites, are named for how they lived rather than for a famous ancestor.
biblical_def: The Hivites occupy two opposite chapters in Israel's story. In Genesis they are the house of Hamor at Shechem, and the record is ugly: “Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her” (Gen 34:2) — the rape of Dinah, and the treacherous massacre by Simeon and Levi that answered it, a crime Jacob was still cursing on his deathbed. In Joshua they are the Gibeonites, and the record is astonishing: alone among the seven nations they refuse to fight. They come in worn shoes and mouldy bread, they lie about their country, and they obtain a covenant. “There was not a city that made peace with the children of Israel, save the Hivites the inhabitants of Gibeon” (Jos 11:19). Israel had sworn, and Israel kept the oath — four hundred years later Saul's breach of it brought famine on the land (2Sa 21:1). The Hivites are also placed in the north, “that dwelt in mount Lebanon” (Jdg 3:3), left in the land to prove Israel. A people under sentence, who sought terms and lived: the deception was sin, but the instinct beneath it was faith in the reports of what the LORD had done.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) reckons the Hivites among the descendants of Canaan and one of the seven nations, noting their seats at Shechem, at Gibeon, and northward under Hermon.
webster_full: HIVITE, n. One of a Canaanitish people descended from Canaan, the son of Ham.
They dwelt about Shechem in the time of Jacob, and at Gibeon in the time of Joshua.
A northern branch inhabited under mount Hermon, in the land of Mizpeh.
The Gibeonites, being Hivites, obtained a league of Joshua by craft, and were made hewers of wood and drawers of water.
Solomon levied a tribute of bond-service upon their remnant.
scriptures: Gen 34:2
And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her.
Jos 9:7
And the men of Israel said unto the Hivites, Peradventure ye dwell among us; and how shall we make a league with you?
There was not a city that made peace with the children of Israel, save the Hivites the inhabitants of Gibeon: all other they took in battle.
Jdg 3:3
Namely, five lords of the Philistines, and all the Canaanites, and the Sidonians, and the Hivites that dwelt in mount Lebanon, from mount Baalhermon unto the entering in of Hamath.
corruption_summary: The Gibeonite league is usually told as a lesson in due diligence; the deeper lesson is that Israel's oath, sworn in error, still bound Israel, because a vow is made to God and not to the beneficiary.
corruption_paragraphs: The moral drawn from Jos 9 in most preaching is a management maxim: check your facts. The text does say it — “the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD” (Jos 9:14) — and the rebuke is real. But the astonishing thing is what follows. The oath was obtained by fraud, and the princes kept it anyway, because they had sworn by the LORD God of Israel and His name was now attached to it. Psa 15 describes the citizen of Zion as one who “sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.” Modern conscience treats a promise as voidable the moment it is discovered to be disadvantageous; the Gibeonites are the standing rebuke.

There is a second thing here that ought not be flattened. Rahab and the Gibeonites are the two Canaanite exceptions, and both acted on the same information — the news of the Red Sea and of Sihon and Og. The Gibeonites confessed it plainly: they had heard what the LORD did in Egypt. Their method was a lie and their fear was slavish rather than filial, and they were reduced to hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God — which is to say, they were brought inside. Judgment falling on a nation never forecloses mercy to the person who seeks terms.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chiwwi (H2340), Hivite, from Chawwah, possibly a tent-village; related in sound though not in sense to chawwah (H2332), Eve, the living.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chiwwi (H2340) — Hivite; sixth son of Canaan in the table of nations (Gen 10:17).
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, a league; the thing the Gibeonites obtained and Israel dared not break.
Hebrew shaba' (H7650) — to swear, literally to seven oneself; the princes' oath in Jos 9:15.
Hebrew chotebe 'etsim — hewers of wood; the servile office assigned them at the altar (Jos 9:21).
Hebrew Gib'on (H1391) — Gibeon, the chief Hivite city, later a high place and the site of Solomon's dream.
usage: “Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite” — the outrage that ruined Simeon and Levi.
“Save the Hivites the inhabitants of Gibeon” — the one city that sued for peace.
“Asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD” — the omission that bound a nation for centuries.

pos: n. pl. (the fifth son of Canaan and his people — the nation of the seven about which Scripture says least)
etymology: From Hebrew Girgashi, the gentilic of Girgash, fifth son of Canaan (Gen 10:16). The meaning is uncertain; a clayey soil has been suggested, but Scripture supplies no gloss and the name is best left unexplained.
biblical_def: The Girgashites are the most obscure of the seven nations of Canaan. They are listed in the table of nations as sprung from Canaan (Gen 10:16), they appear in the full seven-nation roll of Deu 7:1 and in Joshua's promise at Jordan (Jos 3:10), and Nehemiah names them in the great prayer that recites the covenant made with Abraham (Neh 9:8). Beyond the lists, nothing: no city is assigned them, no king is named, no battle is recorded against them. And that is exactly their theological use. The covenant of Gen 15 was sworn over a people Scripture never troubles to describe, and the LORD kept it toward them as exactly as toward the Amorite whose iniquity is measured and the Hittite whose empire is remembered. Nehemiah's prayer is precise about this: God found Abraham's heart faithful, made a covenant to give the land of seven named nations, “and hast performed thy words; for thou art righteous” (Neh 9:8). The Girgashites are the clause of the promise no one would have noticed had it failed — which makes their inclusion in the roll of what was performed the finest possible proof that God does not round off His obligations.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) names the Girgashites among the descendants of Canaan and the nations of the land, remarking that little is recorded of them beyond the enumerations.
webster_full: GIRGASHITE, n. A descendant of Girgash, the fifth son of Canaan.
One of the seven nations of the land of Canaan given by promise to the seed of Abraham.
Their seat is not certainly known; some place them east of the sea of Galilee.
They are named in the covenant of Genesis xv. and in the enumeration of Deuteronomy vii.
Nehemiah recites them among the nations whose land God performed his word to give.
scriptures: And the Jebusite, and the Amorite, and the Girgasite,
Deu 7:1

When the LORD thy God shall bring thee into the land whither thou goest to possess it, and hath cast out many nations before thee, the Hittites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations greater and mightier than thou;
Jos 3:10

And Joshua said, Hereby ye shall know that the living God is among you, and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Hivites, and the Perizzites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites, and the Jebusites.
Neh 9:8

And foundest his heart faithful before thee, and madest a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Jebusites, and the Girgashites, to give it, I say, to his seed, and hast performed thy words; for thou art righteous:
corruption_summary: Obscurity in the record is read as evidence of invention; Scripture treats it as evidence of nothing at all, and keeps the promise to the unremembered nation as exactly as to the famous one.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation the Girgashites expose is not a culture-war one but a scholarly reflex: a name with no attached narrative is quietly reclassified as a filler, a literary device to round the list to seven. The reflex has a poor record — the Hittites were dismissed on the same grounds until the archives at Boghazkoy were read. Scripture is not obliged to narrate every nation it names, and its silences are not confessions.

The principle to recover is the exactness of God's performance. Neh 9:8 does not say that God gave Abraham's seed a fair portion of what was promised; it names seven nations and says “hast performed thy words; for thou art righteous.” Righteousness is the ground given — not generosity, not mercy, but righteousness, the fidelity of one who has bound Himself and will not be found short by a single clause. The believer's hope rests on that same exactness: “For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen” (2Co 1:20).
roots_summary: Hebrew Girgashi (H1622), Girgashite, from Girgash, fifth son of Canaan; meaning uncertain.
roots_lines: Hebrew Girgashi (H1622) — Girgashite; found only in the national lists and the covenant recitals.
Hebrew Kena'an (H3667) — Canaan, their father, whose line fills Gen 10:15-18.
Hebrew karath berith (H3772 + H1285) — to cut a covenant; the transaction of Gen 15 that named them.
Hebrew qum (H6965) — to establish, to make good; used of God performing His word.
Hebrew tsaddiq (H6662) — righteous; Nehemiah's ground for the promise being kept in full.
usage: “And the Girgasite” — a name in the table of nations and almost nowhere else.
“Seven nations greater and mightier than thou” — the roll they complete.
“Hast performed thy words; for thou art righteous” — the accounting Nehemiah gives.

pos: n. (Amorite king of Heshbon, defeated east of Jordan — the first conquest, and the first refrain of Israel's praise)
etymology: From Hebrew Sichon, of uncertain meaning; a sweeping-away or a tempestuous one has been proposed from a root sacha, to sweep. Scripture offers no gloss and the man is known entirely by what he refused.
biblical_def: Sihon king of the Amorites reigned at Heshbon east of Jordan, and Israel asked him only for passage: the king's highway, no turning into field or vineyard, water paid for. He said no, and more than no — “Sihon would not suffer Israel to pass through his border: but Sihon gathered all his people together, and went out against Israel into the wilderness” (Num 21:23). He was destroyed at Jahaz, and his land became the inheritance of Reuben and Gad. Two things make him permanent in Scripture. The first is the explanation Moses gives: “the LORD thy God hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand” (Deu 2:30) — the Pharaoh pattern repeated, a hardening that is God's judicial act and the man's own obstinacy in the same sentence. The second is the liturgy. Sihon and Og became the standing pair in Israel's praise, recited generation after generation in the hallel psalms: “Sihon king of the Amorites: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psa 136:19). The first battle won on the east bank became the proof text sung whenever Israel needed reminding that the God who had begun would finish.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Sihon; the name belongs to sacred history, where it denotes the Amorite king of Heshbon subdued by Moses before the passage of Jordan.
webster_full: SIHON, n. King of the Amorites, whose royal city was Heshbon, beyond Jordan.
He refused Israel a peaceable passage through his coast, and came out against them to Jahaz.
Being smitten, his land from Arnon to Jabbok was possessed by Reuben and Gad.
His overthrow, with that of Og king of Bashan, is repeatedly celebrated in the Psalms.
The prophets recall it as the earnest of the conquest of the whole land.
scriptures: And Sihon would not suffer Israel to pass through his border: but Sihon gathered all his people together, and went out against Israel into the wilderness: and he came to Jahaz, and fought against Israel.
Deu 2:30
But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him: for the LORD thy God hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand, as appeareth this day.
Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan:
Sihon king of the Amorites: for his mercy endureth for ever:
corruption_summary: Deu 2:30 is read as if God overrode a willing man; Scripture says the LORD hardened him and that Sihon himself would not, and asserts both without apology.
corruption_paragraphs: Sihon is one of the texts where the modern reader flinches. If the LORD hardened his spirit, the objection runs, then his refusal was not his own and his destruction was unjust. Scripture will not accept the dilemma. The same verse that says God hardened him says Sihon “would not let us pass”, and Num 21:23 records a free, aggressive, unprovoked muster against a people who had asked for nothing but a road. Paul faces the identical objection head-on in Rom 9 and answers it not by softening the hardening but by denying the objector's standing: “Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God?” (Rom 9:20). The Reformed confession holds both truths without embarrassment — God's decree stands, and the sinner acts freely according to his own nature and is justly condemned for it.

The second corruption is subtler and pastoral: treating Sihon as a curiosity of ancient warfare rather than as the church's appointed memory. Israel did not merely record the victory; Israel sang it, twice over, in the psalms sung at the feasts, and Jephthah argued from it three centuries later. God gives His people specific past deliverances to rehearse precisely because faith is forgetful. A congregation with no habit of reciting what God has actually done for it will meet its next Og with nothing in its mouth.
roots_summary: Hebrew Sichon (H5511), Sihon; his city Cheshbon (H2809), Heshbon, from chashab, to reckon.
roots_lines: Hebrew Sichon (H5511) — Sihon, king of the Amorites at Heshbon.
Hebrew Cheshbon (H2809) — Heshbon, his capital; from a root meaning to reckon or devise.
Hebrew qashah (H7185) — to harden, to make stiff; used of his spirit in Deu 2:30.
Hebrew 'amets (H553) — to make strong or obstinate; the second verb of the same hardening.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, covenant lovingkindness; the refrain attached to his overthrow in Psa 136.
usage: “Sihon would not suffer Israel to pass” — a refusal that cost a kingdom.
“The LORD thy God hardened his spirit” — the Pharaoh pattern east of Jordan.
“Sihon king of the Amorites: for his mercy endureth for ever” — judgment sung as mercy to Israel.

pos: n. (a dynastic name of the kings of Hazor — the northern coalition Joshua burned, and the oppressor Deborah broke)
etymology: From Hebrew Yabin, he understands or he discerns, from bin, to discern. Two kings bear it a century and a half apart, which suggests a throne-name of the house of Hazor rather than a private name.
biblical_def: Jabin is the name on the throne of Hazor, “the head of all those kingdoms” in the north, and it belongs to two men. The first hears of Joshua's southern campaign and assembles the great northern confederacy — “when Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things, that he sent to Jobab king of Madon” (Jos 11:1) — a host with horses and chariots “as the sand that is upon the sea shore”, which Joshua routed at the waters of Merom and whose city he burned. The second reigns in a rebuilt Hazor in the days of the judges: “the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose host was Sisera” (Jdg 4:2). Nine hundred chariots of iron, twenty years of oppression, and then Deborah and Barak and a rainstorm and a river: “So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel” (Jdg 4:23). Asaph still names him in prayer generations later (Psa 83:9). The two Jabins together teach what Judges is for — ground once taken can be lost, and an enemy burned to the foundations can rebuild while the covenant people forget.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Jabin; in sacred history it denotes the kings of Hazor, the first overthrown by Joshua and the second by Deborah and Barak.
webster_full: JABIN, n. King of Hazor, head of the confederacy of northern Canaan destroyed by Joshua at the waters of Merom.
The name signifies one who understands or discerns.
A second Jabin, reigning in Hazor in the days of the judges, oppressed Israel twenty years.
His captain was Sisera, who had nine hundred chariots of iron.
He was subdued by the hand of Deborah and Barak, and his memory is invoked in the eighty-third Psalm.
scriptures: Jos 11:1
And it came to pass, when Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things, that he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph,
Jdg 4:2
And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose host was Sisera, which dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles.
Jdg 4:23
So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel.
Psa 83:9
Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison:
corruption_summary: Judges is read as a cycle of political misfortune; the text says the LORD sold them, which makes the oppressor a rod in a Father's hand rather than an accident of geopolitics.
corruption_paragraphs: Jdg 4:2 will not permit a merely political reading of Israel's troubles: “the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin.” The verb is commercial and deliberate. Israel was not overrun because Hazor had better metallurgy; Israel was handed over, by God, for covenant unfaithfulness, exactly as Deu 28 had said in advance. Modern historiography reverses this — the theology is treated as a later interpretive gloss laid over the real causes, which are chariots and trade routes. Scripture treats the chariots as the instrument and the covenant as the cause, and the whole book of Judges is unintelligible on any other reading.

The second Jabin also rebukes a triumphalism that assumes ground once won stays won. Joshua burned Hazor; Judges finds a Jabin reigning in Hazor again. Nothing in the conquest was undone by God; it was undone by a generation “which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel” (Jdg 2:10). Reformation in a church, a family, or a nation is held only by teaching — and the enemy is patient enough to rebuild on his own ashes while the covenant people neglect to catechise their children.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yabin (H2985), Jabin, from bin (H995), to discern; his city Chatsor (H2674), Hazor, an enclosure.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yabin (H2985) — Jabin; probably a dynastic title of the kings of Hazor.
Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, understand; the root of the name, ironic in a king who could not read the times.
Hebrew Chatsor (H2674) — Hazor, an enclosure or castle; “the head of all those kingdoms” (Jos 11:10).
Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; the LORD's own act in Jdg 4:2, judgment by handing over.
Hebrew kana' (H3665) — to subdue, humble; God's act in Jdg 4:23, the reversal of the selling.
usage: “Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things” — the northern coalition forming.
“The LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin” — oppression as covenant discipline.
“As to Sisera, as to Jabin” — a prayer that recites old deliverances.

pos: n. (the nation sprung from Lot's younger daughter — Israel's kinsman, spared by divine command and hostile for a thousand years)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ammon, from 'am, a people or kinsman; the name given by Lot's younger daughter to her son Benammi, “son of my people” (Gen 19:38). The nation is almost always called bene-'Ammon, the children of Ammon.
biblical_def: Ammon is the nation descended from Lot by his younger daughter, and its whole history is governed by that kinship. Israel was expressly forbidden to touch them: “distress them not, nor meddle with them: for I will not give thee of the land of the children of Ammon any possession; because I have given it unto the children of Lot” (Deu 2:19). God parcels out land to nations outside the covenant and defends their borders. Ammon returned nothing for it. They hired Balaam, they refused Israel bread and water, they besieged Jabesh-gilead and offered to thrust out every right eye, they warred on Jephthah, they humiliated David's ambassadors, and they joined the coalition against Jehoshaphat (2Ch 20:1). Amos indicts a specific atrocity: “because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border” (Amo 1:13) — the murder of the unborn to gain land. Zephaniah sentences them with Moab to be as Sodom and Gomorrah (Zep 2:9), a fitting end for the seed of Lot. Their god was Milcom or Molech, and Solomon built him a high place. Yet the door was not sealed: Naamah the Ammonitess was the mother of Rehoboam, and so an Ammonite woman stands in the royal line.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Ammon as a nation; in sacred geography it denotes the people descended from Benammi, son of Lot, dwelling east of Gilead, whose capital was Rabbah.
webster_full: AMMON, n. The son of Lot by his younger daughter, called Benammi; and from him, the nation of the Ammonites.
They dwelt east of the Jordan and of the Amorites, between the Arnon and the Jabbok, having Rabbah for their chief city.
Their idol was Milcom, or Molech, to whom children were made to pass through the fire.
By the law an Ammonite might not enter into the congregation of the Lord unto the tenth generation.
They were subdued by David, and their overthrow is foretold by the prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos and Zephaniah.
scriptures: Deu 2:19

And when thou comest nigh over against the children of Ammon, distress them not, nor meddle with them: for I will not give thee of the land of the children of Ammon any possession; because I have given it unto the children of Lot for a possession.
It came to pass after this also, that the children of Moab, and the children of Ammon, and with them other beside the Ammonites, came against Jehoshaphat to battle.
Amo 1:13

Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border:
Zep 2:9

Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them.
corruption_summary: Amos indicts Ammon for killing the unborn to enlarge a border; the same act, renamed, is defended today as a private matter, and the prophet's category of national bloodguilt is dismissed as primitive.
corruption_paragraphs: Amo 1:13 is one of the plainest verses in the prophets on the killing of children in the womb, and it is worth stating exactly what it says. The charge is not idolatry, not aggression in general, but a specific method: they ripped up the women with child, and the motive given is territorial gain — “that they might enlarge their border.” The LORD treats it as one of the atrocities for which a nation outside the covenant is destroyed. Ammon was never given the law of Sinai; the judgment falls under the law written on the conscience, which Paul says leaves the Gentiles “without excuse” (Rom 1:20). The modern defence of abortion trades on the unborn child being invisible and the reason being private; the prophet answers on both counts at once, naming the deed publicly and reckoning it to the nation.

The second thing Ammon exposes is how a kinsman becomes the bitterest enemy. Lot chose the plain of Jordan by sight; his line ends as the breeding of nettles. Yet Deu 2:19 stands: God gave Ammon land and forbade Israel to take it, which is a standing rebuke to any theology that treats the nations as mere scenery for the covenant people. And Deu 23:3 stands with it — “An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD” — and yet Ruth the Moabitess did, and Naamah the Ammonitess bore a king. Law and mercy are not at odds; mercy comes through the covenant, not around it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Ammon (H5983), from 'am (H5971), people; Ben-'Ammi (H1151), son of my people, the child of Gen 19:38.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Ammon (H5983) — Ammon; almost always in the phrase bene-'Ammon, children of Ammon.
Hebrew Ben-'Ammi (H1151) — Benammi, “son of my people”; the name given by Lot's younger daughter.
Hebrew Milkom (H4445) — Milcom, the Ammonite idol, called the abomination of the Ammonites (1Ki 11:5).
Hebrew Rabbah (H7237) — Rabbah, their capital, taken by Joab and David (2Sa 12:26-29).
Hebrew gabal / gebul (H1366) — a border; the thing Ammon killed children to enlarge (Amo 1:13).
usage: “Distress them not, nor meddle with them” — a border God defended for Lot's sake.
“They have ripped up the women with child of Gilead” — the atrocity Amos names.
“The children of Ammon as Gomorrah” — the sentence upon Lot's line.

pos: n. (Philistine king of Gath — the pagan who twice sheltered David, and the refuge that nearly cost him everything)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Akiysh, of uncertain and probably Philistine derivation. He is called Abimelech in the title of Psa 34, which appears to be a Philistine royal title as Pharaoh was Egyptian.
biblical_def: Achish king of Gath appears at the two lowest points of David's exile. The first time David comes alone and in terror — “David arose, and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath” (1Sa 21:10) — carrying, of all things, the sword of Goliath of Gath. Recognised and afraid, he feigned madness and scrabbled on the gate, and Psa 34 and Psa 56 came out of that humiliation. The second time he comes with six hundred men and a settled unbelief: “I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul”, and so “David arose, and he passed over with the six hundred men that were with him unto Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath” (1Sa 27:2). For sixteen months the LORD's anointed lived as a Philistine vassal at Ziklag, raiding southern tribes and lying to his lord about it, and was marched out to fight against Israel until the Philistine princes refused him. Achish's own words are the sharpest rebuke in the story: “I know that thou art good in my sight, as an angel of God” (1Sa 29:9) — a heathen king's trust, earned by systematic deceit. A later Achish still reigns at Gath in Solomon's day (1Ki 2:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Achish; in sacred history it is the name of the Philistine king of Gath with whom David twice took refuge, called Abimelech in the title of the thirty-fourth Psalm.
webster_full: ACHISH, n. A king of Gath, one of the five lordships of the Philistines.
David fled to him from Saul, and being known, feigned himself mad before him.
Returning a second time with six hundred men, he received of Achish the city of Ziklag.
Achish would have taken him to battle against Israel, but the princes of the Philistines refused him.
A king of the same name at Gath in the days of Solomon received the runaway servants of Shimei.
scriptures: And David arose, and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath.
And David arose, and he passed over with the six hundred men that were with him unto Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath.
And Achish answered and said to David, I know that thou art good in my sight, as an angel of God: notwithstanding the princes of the Philistines have said, He shall not go up with us to the battle.
And it came to pass at the end of three years, that two of the servants of Shimei ran away unto Achish son of Maachah king of Gath. And they told Shimei, saying, Behold, thy servants be in Gath.
corruption_summary: The Ziklag years are smoothed into a shrewd survival strategy; Scripture presents them as sixteen months of unbelief that began with a sentence David said in his heart and God had never said.
corruption_paragraphs: David among the Philistines is the standing test of whether a reader will let Scripture indict its heroes. Popular treatments make Ziklag a clever manoeuvre — the fugitive hiding where his pursuer dare not follow. The text is blunter. It gives the reason in David's own interior speech: “I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul: there is nothing better for me than that I should speedily escape into the land of the Philistines” (1Sa 27:1). That was false, and David had a prophet, an ephod, and a covenant word that he would be king. What follows is the fruit of it: raiding, slaughter to leave no witnesses, systematic lying, and a march toward the field where Saul and Jonathan would die. Scripture is not embarrassed to record that the man after God's own heart spent more than a year in practical apostasy, and it does not moralise; it simply lets the sequel — Ziklag burned, his men speaking of stoning him — do the work, until “David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (1Sa 30:6).

The second corruption is to make Achish the villain. He is not. He is a courteous pagan who gives a homeless man a city and speaks of him as an angel of God, and every word of that trust rests on lies. The believer's witness before unbelievers is a real trust, and it can be purchased with deceit and then spent. When Achish says “I know that thou art good in my sight”, the reader should wince, not applaud.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Akiysh (H397), Achish, of Philistine origin; Gath (H1661), a winepress; 'Abimelek (H40), my father is king, apparently the Philistine royal style.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Akiysh (H397) — Achish; borne by at least two kings of Gath a century apart.
Hebrew Gath (H1661) — Gath, a winepress; one of the five Philistine lordships and Goliath's city.
Hebrew 'Abimelek (H40) — Abimelech, the title used of him in the inscription of Psa 34.
Hebrew Tsiqlag (H6860) — Ziklag, the city Achish gave David, later reckoned to the kings of Judah.
Hebrew halal (H1984) — in one stem, to act madly; the feigned madness of 1Sa 21:13.
usage: “Fled that day for fear of Saul” — the flight that produced two psalms.
“Unto Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath” — the second and longer surrender.
“As an angel of God” — a pagan's praise built on deceit.

pos: n. (king of Tyre, ally of David and Solomon — the Gentile who sent cedar for the house of God; also the craftsman of the same name)
etymology: From Hebrew Chiram or Chirom, a contraction of Achiram, my brother is exalted, from 'ach, brother, and rum, to be high. Chronicles spells it Churam, Huram.
biblical_def: Hiram king of Tyre is the friendliest Gentile in the Old Testament. He sent messengers and cedar and workmen to build David a house (1Ch 14:1), and when Solomon succeeded, Hiram moved first: “Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants unto Solomon; for he had heard that they had anointed him king in the room of his father: for Hiram was ever a lover of David” (1Ki 5:1). His answer to Solomon's request for timber is a confession no Israelite prompted: “Blessed be the LORD this day, which hath given unto David a wise son over this great people” (1Ki 5:7). Chronicles records the same in writing: “Because the LORD hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them” (2Ch 2:11). Cedar and fir from Lebanon, rafted down the coast to Joppa; masons and hewers working beside Solomon's levy; wheat and oil sent back year by year; “and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon; and they two made a league together” (1Ki 5:12). A second Hiram, the brass-worker of Tyre whose mother was of the tribe of Naphtali, cast the two pillars, the sea, and all the vessels. The temple that housed the glory of the God of Israel was raised with Gentile timber by Gentile hands — a fact the prophets would later make into a promise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hiram; in sacred history it names the king of Tyre, friend of David and Solomon, and also the Tyrian artificer in brass who wrought the vessels of the temple.
webster_full: HIRAM, n. A king of Tyre, contemporary with David and Solomon, and a lover of David all his days.
He furnished cedar and fir from Lebanon and skilful workmen for the building of the temple.
Solomon gave him yearly wheat and pure oil, and afterward twenty cities in Galilee, which pleased him not.
Also, a workman in brass, the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali by a man of Tyre.
This Hiram cast the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea, and the vessels of the house of the Lord.
scriptures: And Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants unto Solomon; for he had heard that they had anointed him king in the room of his father: for Hiram was ever a lover of David.
And it came to pass, when Hiram heard the words of Solomon, that he rejoiced greatly, and said, Blessed be the LORD this day, which hath given unto David a wise son over this great people.
Then Huram the king of Tyre answered in writing, which he sent to Solomon, Because the LORD hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them.
And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him: and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon; and they two made a league together.
corruption_summary: Hiram has been drafted into the founding legend of speculative freemasonry, where the temple's craftsman is murdered and raised in a mystery rite that Scripture knows nothing of.
corruption_paragraphs: The largest corruption attached to this name has nothing to do with modern academia. Speculative freemasonry, from the eighteenth century onward, built its central legend around Hiram Abiff, the widow's son of 1Ki 7:13-14, recast as a master builder murdered for refusing to divulge a secret word and ceremonially raised again. Scripture records no such thing: the craftsman finishes his work, the vessels are numbered, and he leaves the narrative alive and unremarkable. The invention matters because of what it does with the temple — it converts the house where blood was shed for sin into a lodge where a secret is transmitted, and it offers a counterfeit resurrection detached from Christ. The dictionary names it as a fabrication laid on a biblical name, and notes that the true Widow's Son is the One who was really killed and really raised.

The honest corruption to name in Hiram of Tyre is more ordinary: alliance. His friendship was genuine and God used it, and Scripture never rebukes Solomon for the league. But Tyre's later history — Jezebel came from that coast, and Ezekiel would sing the great lament over the prince of Tyrus — shows how a trading partnership becomes a religious one. The temple was built with Tyrian cedar; within two generations Baal of Tyre had an altar in Samaria. Good alliances need watching precisely because they are good.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chiram / Churam (H2438, H2361), Hiram or Huram, from 'ach (H251), brother, and rum (H7311), to be high.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chiram (H2438) — Hiram; the Kings spelling of the Tyrian king's name.
Hebrew Churam (H2361) — Huram; the Chronicles spelling of the same name, used of both king and craftsman.
Hebrew Tsor (H6865) — Tyre, a rock; the island fortress and trading city of Phoenicia.
Hebrew 'erez (H730) — cedar; the timber of Lebanon that panelled the house of the LORD.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, league; the treaty between Hiram and Solomon (1Ki 5:12).
usage: “Hiram was ever a lover of David” — a Gentile friendship that outlived a reign.
“Blessed be the LORD this day” — a heathen king blessing the God of Israel.
“They two made a league together” — cedar for wheat, and a temple raised.
